reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: A rare disorder in which the liver contains multiple blood-filled cystic cavities scattered through the parenchyma
It is frequently asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, but can cause hepatomegaly, deranged liver tests, or, uncommonly, life-threatening intra-abdominal haemorrhage from rupture
Recognised associations include anabolic androgenic steroids, oestrogens and oral contraceptives, azathioprine and other immunosuppressants, and chronic wasting or malignant disease
In immunocompromised patients, infection with Bartonella species (bacillary peliosis/angiomatosis) is an important and treatable cause
Imaging appearances can mimic vascular tumours or metastases, so the diagnosis is often uncertain without histology
Biopsy of the lesions carries a bleeding risk because the cavities are blood-filled, and this must be weighed carefully
Withdrawal of a causative drug frequently leads to regression of the lesions
The principal danger is spontaneous rupture with haemoperitoneum, which is a surgical and radiological emergency
reference.pathophysiology: Peliosis hepatis is characterised by dilated, blood-filled sinusoidal spaces or cystic cavities within the liver parenchyma, resulting from disruption of the sinusoidal endothelial lining and the supporting reticulin framework. Injury to sinusoidal endothelium, together with outflow obstruction at the level of small hepatic venules and focal hepatocellular necrosis, is thought to allow blood to pool in expanding lacunar spaces. A range of hormonal agents, immunosuppressive drugs, chronic debilitating illness, and, in the immunocompromised, Bartonella infection can trigger this endothelial injury. The thin-walled, engorged cavities are fragile and may rupture, producing potentially catastrophic haemorrhage, while extensive involvement can impair liver function or contribute to portal hypertension.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) to characterise the lesions and exclude tumour
Careful drug and hormone history, including anabolic steroids and immunosuppressants
Serology or molecular testing for Bartonella in immunocompromised patients
Liver function tests to assess hepatic involvement
Cautious tissue sampling only when necessary, given bleeding risk
Assessment for underlying malignancy or chronic wasting illness
redFlags: Spontaneous rupture with intraperitoneal bleeding and haemodynamic instability requiring emergency intervention
Rapidly enlarging liver with pain suggesting expanding lesions
Signs of hepatic failure with extensive parenchymal involvement
Bartonella infection in an immunocompromised host requiring prompt antimicrobial treatment
reference.prognosis: Many cases are asymptomatic and regress once a causative drug or infection is removed or treated; prognosis worsens markedly with spontaneous rupture and haemorrhage or when there is extensive parenchymal involvement or an aggressive underlying illness.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lesions for a vascular tumour or metastasis and mismanaging accordingly
Performing biopsy without accounting for the significant bleeding risk
Failing to identify and stop a causative drug
Overlooking treatable Bartonella infection in immunocompromised patients
